purpose.title: Purpose and voluntariness
purpose.body: In the LLARS research project at the Centre for Artificial Intelligence (KIZ) of Nuremberg Institute of Technology Georg Simon Ohm we investigate how well current language models match the responses of trained online counsellors. Your judgements (preference comparisons between two anonymised responses) feed into scientific publications (e.g. EMNLP, ACL) and inform when AI can responsibly assist counselling. Participation is fully voluntary; no disadvantage arises from non-participation or later withdrawal.

data.title: Data we process
data.body: (a) Account data: username, email address, chosen language, timestamps. (b) Study data: your evaluation choices, presentation order, technical metadata (browser type, IP address — hashed before storage). (c) Optional and voluntary: basic demographic information. We collect no counselling data from you — all comparison examples in the study originate from research-released corpora. Before any analysis your identity is pseudonymised (separation of identity and evaluation data per §22(2) BDSG).

legal.title: Legal basis
legal.body: Processing of your data takes place on the basis of your consent pursuant to Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR. Insofar as special categories of personal data are affected (e.g. through voluntary demographic information) we additionally rely on Art. 9(2)(a) + (j) GDPR in conjunction with §27(1) BDSG (research privilege) and Art. 89(1) GDPR. Technical and organisational safeguards under §22(2) BDSG (in particular pseudonymisation and access control) apply. This research follows the DFG Code 'Guidelines for Safeguarding Good Research Practice' and the ethics guidelines of TH Nürnberg.

recipients.title: Recipients and data transfers
recipients.body: Aggregated, anonymised results are published exclusively in scientific venues (e.g. EMNLP, ACL). NO row-level dataset release on Zenodo, HuggingFace or comparable repositories takes place. Internal recipients are limited to the researchers at TH Nürnberg directly involved in the study. No transfers to third countries take place. Reuse of the pseudonymised data for topically related follow-up studies within the same research line at KIZ (Recital 33 GDPR) is covered by this consent.

retention.title: Retention
retention.body: Pseudonymised evaluation data are stored, in line with the DFG guidelines and §27(1) BDSG, for up to ten years after the end of the study, for reproducibility and archival purposes. Account credentials are deleted on withdrawal of consent or at the latest twelve months after the end of the study. Results already published in aggregated, anonymised form cannot be retracted — Art. 17(3)(d) GDPR permits this research exemption.

rights.title: Your rights
rights.body: You have, at any time, the right to: (1) access (Art. 15 GDPR), (2) rectification (Art. 16), (3) erasure (Art. 17, subject to the exemption above under Art. 17(3)(d)), (4) restriction of processing (Art. 18), (5) data portability (Art. 20), (6) objection (Art. 21), and (7) withdrawal of your consent at any time without giving reasons, with effect for the future (Art. 7(3)). Withdrawal does not affect the lawfulness of processing carried out before withdrawal. No automated decision-making including profiling within the meaning of Art. 22 GDPR takes place. You may lodge a complaint with the Bavarian Data Protection Authority: BayLDA, Promenade 18, 91522 Ansbach, poststelle{'@'}lda.bayern.de.

privacyPolicy.title: Privacy Policy (as of 07/2026)
privacyPolicy.intro: The protection of your personal data is important to us. In accordance with Art. 13 and 14 GDPR, we inform you below about which data we process when you use the LLARS platform, for what purposes and on what legal basis.

controller.title: 1. Who is responsible for data processing?

dataCollection.title: 2. Which data is collected and why?
dataCollection.paragraph1: When you merely visit the website, we initially only process the data that your browser transmits automatically (see Server log files). In addition, we process data that you actively enter as well as – subject to your consent – usage data for audience measurement.
dataCollection.paragraph2: LLARS is a research platform for evaluating and analysing AI-generated content. By using it, the data you enter and the data collected during evaluations is processed for scientific research purposes and – where possible – pseudonymised or anonymised. The legal basis is the performance of a task carried out in the public (research) interest under Art. 6(1)(e) GDPR in conjunction with Art. 4 BayDSG, and for special categories of data Art. 9(2)(j) GDPR in conjunction with Art. 25 BayDSG (research privilege); for study participation additionally your consent under Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR.

serverLogs.title: 3. Server log files
serverLogs.text: When the website is accessed, the server automatically collects information transmitted by your browser (including IP address, date and time of access, page accessed, browser and operating system used). This data serves the technical operation, security and stability of the platform and is deleted or anonymised after a short period.
serverLogs.legalBasis: Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(e) GDPR in conjunction with Art. 4 BayDSG (performance of a task carried out in the public interest) and our legitimate interest in secure operation (Art. 6(1)(f) GDPR).

cookies.title: 4. Cookies and local storage
cookies.text: We use technically necessary cookies and local storage (localStorage) that are required to operate the platform – for example to manage your login session, for language settings and to store your consent decisions. We set these necessary cookies without separate consent on the basis of Section 25(2) TDDDG.
cookies.optional: Non-essential cookies or processing (e.g. audience measurement, map service) are only used after your consent, which you give via the cookie notice and can withdraw at any time.

analytics.title: 5. Audience measurement with Matomo
analytics.text: For statistical analysis of usage we use the open-source software Matomo, which we operate ourselves on servers of TH Nürnberg – no data is transferred to third parties. Matomo is operated cookie-free and with a shortened IP address by default.
analytics.consent: Audience measurement only takes place after you have consented via the cookie notice. Without your consent, no analysis is carried out. Your decision is stored locally in your browser; you can withdraw it at any time by clearing your browser's local storage.
analytics.legalBasis: Legal basis: your consent under Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR and Section 25(1) TDDDG.

maps.title: 6. Map display (Google Maps)
maps.text: On the contact page we embed a map from Google Maps (provider: Google Ireland Limited, Gordon House, Barrow Street, Dublin 4, Ireland). The map is only loaded after you have actively consented to loading it (two-click solution). No connection to Google is established beforehand.
maps.consent: When the map is loaded, data – in particular your IP address – is transmitted to Google and may be transferred to third countries (USA). The transfer is based on the EU Commission's standard contractual clauses. Your consent is stored locally in your browser and can be withdrawn at any time.
maps.legalBasis: Legal basis: your consent under Art. 6(1)(a) GDPR and Section 25(1) TDDDG. Further information: Google's privacy policy.

account.title: 7. Account, login and authentication
account.text: A user account is required to use protected features and can only be created via an invitation code. Login and account management are handled via the self-hosted open-source solution Authentik. We process your username, an encrypted password, an optional display name and – if provided – your email address, as well as session and log data to secure the login.
account.legalBasis: Legal basis: Art. 6(1)(b) GDPR (performance of the usage relationship) or Art. 6(1)(e) GDPR in conjunction with Art. 4 BayDSG.

email.title: 8. Sending of emails
email.text: To send invitation, notification and system messages we use an email delivery service provider as a processor. The data required for delivery (email address, message content) is processed. A data processing agreement pursuant to Art. 28 GDPR is in place with the provider.

recipients.title: 9. Who receives my data?
recipients.paragraph1: Your data is used internally for research and development within the LLARS project. It is disclosed to third parties only where legally required, where you have expressly consented, or where technically necessary to use the services mentioned above (map service, email delivery).
recipients.paragraph2: The servers for this project are hosted on machines of Technische Hochschule Nürnberg. Data processing agreements pursuant to Art. 28 GDPR have been concluded with the processors involved to ensure data protection compliance.

retention.title: 10. How long is my data stored?
retention.text: We store personal data only for as long as necessary for the stated purposes. Server log files are deleted or anonymised in the short term. Account data is stored for the duration of your account and removed after its deletion, unless statutory retention obligations apply. Research data is processed according to the respective study and consent context and subsequently anonymised or deleted.

protection.title: 11. How is my data protected?
protection.paragraph1: We take technical and organisational measures to protect your data. These include in particular encryption of transmission (TLS), role-based access control and encrypted storage of credentials.

rights.title: 12. What rights do I have?
rights.paragraph1: You have the right to access (Art. 15 GDPR), rectification (Art. 16), erasure (Art. 17), restriction of processing (Art. 18), data portability (Art. 20) and the right to object to processing (Art. 21 GDPR). You can withdraw consent you have given at any time with effect for the future.
rights.complaint: Independently of this, you have the right to lodge a complaint with a data protection supervisory authority (Art. 77 GDPR). The competent authority is the Bavarian Data Protection Commissioner (BayLfD), Wagmüllerstraße 18, 80538 Munich, Germany.
rights.contact: To exercise your rights, please use the contact details provided above.

frobenius.title: Frobenius distance
frobenius.whatIs: The Frobenius norm measures the overall difference between two matrices as the Euclidean distance of all matrix elements.
frobenius.exampleIntro: If we compare the transition matrices of pillar 1 (role plays) and pillar 3 (anonymized data):

examples.item1: A Frobenius distance of 0.1 means the counseling patterns are very similar
examples.item2: A distance of 0.5 shows clear differences in communication transitions
examples.item3: The larger the value, the more differently counselors behave across the data sources

frobenius.source: Golub, G.H. & Van Loan, C.F. (2013). Matrix Computations (4th ed.). Johns Hopkins University Press.

jsd.title: Jensen-Shannon divergence (JSD)
jsd.whatIs: JSD is a symmetric measure of the difference between two probability distributions. It is based on Kullback-Leibler divergence, but symmetric and always defined.
jsd.exampleIntro: For each row of the transition matrix (each source state) we compute the JSD:

examples.item1: If a counselor after an "Active listening" intervention (CO-IF-AC) in pillar 1 usually moves to "Questions" but in pillar 3 to "Informing", the JSD for this row shows a high value
examples.item2: Average JSD near 0: the transition patterns are almost identical
examples.item3: Average JSD near 1: the transition patterns are completely different

jsd.source: Lin, J. (1991). Divergence measures based on the Shannon entropy. IEEE Transactions on Information Theory, 37(1), 145-151.

permutation.title: Permutation test
permutation.whatIs: A non-parametric significance test that checks the null hypothesis that two matrices come from the same distribution.

steps.step1: Compute the observed Frobenius distance between the original matrices
steps.step2: Randomly mix the count data of both matrices
steps.step3: Compute the Frobenius distance of the mixed matrices
steps.step5: p-value = proportion of permutations with distance >= observed distance

permutation.exampleIntro: We test whether the differences between role plays (pillar 1) and real counseling sessions (pillar 3) are statistically significant:

examples.item1: p < 0.05: The differences are significant - role plays do not perfectly mirror real counseling
examples.item2: p >= 0.05: No significant difference detected - the data sources may show the same patterns

permutation.source: Good, P. (2005). Permutation, Parametric and Bootstrap Tests of Hypotheses (3rd ed.). Springer.

effect.title: Effect size
effect.whatIs: Effect size indicates how large a difference is in practice, independent of sample size. A significant difference can be small when the sample is very large.
effect.normalizedNote: where n, m are the matrix dimensions
effect.exampleIntro: Even if the permutation test is significant (p < 0.05), the effect size shows whether the difference is practically relevant:

examples.item1: Small effect size (< 0.2): The differences are statistical but hardly relevant in practice - counselors behave similarly
examples.item2: Medium effect size (0.2 - 0.5): Noticeable differences in counseling patterns
examples.item3: Large effect size (> 0.5): Clearly different counseling styles between the data sources

effect.source: Cohen, J. (1988). Statistical Power Analysis for the Behavioral Sciences (2nd ed.). Routledge.

chiSquare.title: Chi-square test for Markov chains
chiSquare.whatIs: The chi-square test checks for each source state whether the transition probabilities differ significantly.
chiSquare.formulaNote: where O = observed, E = expected frequencies
chiSquare.exampleIntro: For each counseling code (e.g. CO-IF-AC "Active listening") we test separately:

examples.item1: If after "Active listening" in pillar 1 60% move to "Questions" but in pillar 3 only 40%, the chi-square test shows whether this difference is significant
examples.item2: This shows exactly which counseling techniques differ between data sources

chiSquare.interpretationIntro: The share of significant states (p < 0.05) shows how many counseling techniques differ:
chiSquare.source: Anderson, T.W. & Goodman, L.A. (1957). Statistical inference about Markov chains. The Annals of Mathematical Statistics, 28(1), 89-110.

laplace.title: Laplace smoothing (additive smoothing)
laplace.whatIs: Laplace smoothing prevents issues with zero counts in the matrix by adding a small value to all cells.
laplace.exampleIntro: If a specific transition (e.g. "Questions" -> "Confrontation") never occurs in pillar 1 but occurs 5 times in pillar 3:

examples.item1: Without smoothing: division by zero possible, JSD = infinity
examples.item2: With alpha = 1: each cell gets at least 1 pseudo-count
examples.item3: Higher alpha: more conservative estimate but smooths real differences

recommended.title: Recommended values
recommended.alphaZero: alpha = 0: No smoothing (only with complete data)

laplace.source: Manning, C.D., Raghavan, P. & Schuetze, H. (2008). Introduction to Information Retrieval. Cambridge University Press.

tooltips.agreementMetrics: Statistical measures of inter-rater reliability - how consistently multiple evaluators rate the same items
tooltips.cohensKappa: Measures agreement between exactly 2 raters, adjusting for chance agreement. Considers how often raters would agree randomly.
tooltips.krippendorffAlpha: A robust measure suitable for any number of raters, missing data, and various data types. The standard metric for content analysis.
tooltips.fleissKappa: Extension of Cohen's Kappa for 3 or more raters. Measures agreement across all evaluators simultaneously.
tooltips.percentAgreement: Simple percentage of cases where evaluators agreed. Easy to interpret but doesn't account for chance agreement.

icc.title: ICC (Intraclass Correlation)
icc.description: Measures the reliability of ratings by comparing between-rater variance to total variance. Ideal for continuous rating scales.

kendallW.title: Kendall's W (Coefficient of Concordance)
kendallW.description: Measures agreement among multiple raters when ranking items. Values range from 0 (no agreement) to 1 (complete agreement).

kendallTau.name: Kendall's Tau
kendallTau.description: Measures ordinal association between rankings. More robust than Spearman for small sample sizes.

mae.title: MAE (Mean Absolute Error)
mae.description: Average absolute difference between predictions and ground truth. Lower values indicate better agreement.

rmse.title: RMSE (Root Mean Squared Error)
rmse.description: Square root of average squared differences. More sensitive to outliers than MAE. Lower values indicate better agreement.

macroF1.title: Macro F1 Score
macroF1.description: Average F1 score across all classes, treating each class equally regardless of frequency. Good for balanced evaluation.

microF1.title: Micro F1 Score
microF1.description: F1 score calculated by aggregating true positives across all classes. Weighted by class frequency.

tooltips.dimensionDistribution: Shows the distribution of ratings for each dimension. Heatmap colors indicate relative frequency.
tooltips.spiderChart: Compares average ratings between humans and LLMs across all dimensions. Larger areas = higher average values.
tooltips.interRaterAgreement: Shows pairwise agreement between all raters. Green = high agreement, Red = low agreement. Calculated as the proportion of exactly matching ratings (rounded to integers).
tooltips.bucketDistribution: Shows how many items were assigned to each bucket (Good/Medium/Bad). Aggregated across all human and LLM evaluators.
tooltips.provenanceAnalysis: Compares where rated content came from (generation LLM, prompt, and prompt+LLM pair) and highlights which origins most often end up in the top bucket. Format x/y = top-bucket hits divided by all assignments for that origin.
tooltips.ratingProvenanceAnalysis: Compares where rated content came from (generation LLM, prompt, and prompt+LLM pair) and highlights which origins currently achieve the highest normalized rating scores.
tooltips.conversationProvenance: Analyzes conversation partner combinations. Derives who wrote the counselor and client messages (Human vs AI) and shows which combinations achieve the best ratings. Format: Counselor × Client.
tooltips.authenticityProvenance: Shows how well each LLM generation source fools evaluators. Fool rate = percentage of votes that incorrectly classified fake content as real. Higher fool rate means the LLM generates more convincing fake content.
tooltips.rankingAgreement: Per summary: Did both evaluators place it in the same bucket? Counted as: Matching summaries / Co-rated summaries. Metrics use ordinal calculation (Bucket-Krippendorff).
tooltips.kappaMatrix: Chance-corrected agreement (Cohen's kappa) for every rater pair. Unlike the plain agreement heatmap, this removes the agreement expected by chance alone. Rules of thumb: ≥ 0.61 substantial, ≥ 0.81 almost perfect.
